statement: Three case reports from one US psychiatric hospital in a single year (Rainey & Crowder, 1975) describe young men, aged 18 and 19, who after street drugs sold as PCP, THC or methadone, and presumed by the authors to contain phencyclidine, had psychoses lasting 2 to 4 weeks: agitation, hostility, disorientation, unsteadiness, insensitivity to pain in one, hearing voices in two, and dangerous behaviour (one jumped from a third-floor window, landing uninjured; one kicked a window until its frame came loose); afterwards they remembered little or nothing of the illness, two of them nothing of the first two weeks. All three recovered within 2 to 4 weeks, one after he left the hospital on his own, and none showed psychosis at the last assessment reported (days to a month later), although one man's psychological tests at 13 days suggested a schizophrenic process with organic impairment that had improved a month later. The authors note that in earlier reports PCP's mind-altering effects usually lasted 18 to 24 hours and that only a few longer reactions were known. They could not say why their patients were ill for so long, and list possible reasons: the dose, slow breakdown of the drug, toxic breakdown products, individual sensitivity, or the drug setting off or worsening a schizophrenic process. No drug test confirmed PCP, the men's psychiatric histories are not given, and three case reports cannot show how often this happens or why. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Doctors in 1975 described three young men who were in hospital for two to four weeks with a severe mental breakdown (psychosis) after street drugs they thought were PCP. They were confused, angry and heard voices, and one jumped from a high window. All three got better, and afterwards remembered little or nothing of their illness. Their drugs were never tested, and three cases cannot show how often this happens.
population: Three young men (aged 18 and 19) admitted to one psychiatric hospital in Detroit within a year
exposure: Street drugs sold as PCP, THC or methadone, presumed by the authors to contain phencyclidine; no toxicology (amounts, where known, are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: None; the authors compare with the usual duration of PCP effects reported in earlier studies
outcome: Duration and features of psychosis, recovery and memory of the episode
magnitude: Three cases; psychosis lasting 2 to 4 weeks (case 1 oriented without psychosis 14 days after the drug; case 2 improving from about 5 days after admission with amnesia for 2 weeks; case 3 psychotic until he left hospital on its 17th day); usual psychotomimetic effects 18 to 24 hours, as cited from earlier literature.

evidence.locator: Case Reports, Case 1 (p. 1076, both columns, to p. 1077, left column top)
evidence.extracted: A 19-year-old man, said by an anonymous caller to have taken PCP, was transferred 4 days later mute, staring, salivating and insensitive to pinprick; after seizure-like episodes he became assaultive and was secluded; 11 days after the drug he was more cooperative and 3 days later oriented with no psychotic signs, remembering nothing of the first 2 weeks.

evidence.locator: Case Reports, Case 2, 1st to 4th paragraphs (left column)
evidence.extracted: An 18-year-old man who took a drug sold as THC came to the emergency room after 30 more hours without sleep, hostile, suspicious, ataxic, disoriented and hearing chains; the day after admission he jumped from a third-floor window, landing uninjured; after 4 more days he became more aware and remembered nothing of the previous 2 weeks. Tests 13 days after the drug suggested a chronic schizophrenic process with residual organic impairment; a month later there was no psychosis and the impairment had improved. Three of his four friends were hospitalized and discharged within 2 to 3 days.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

evidence.locator: Case Reports, Case 3 (left column, lower part, and right column)
evidence.extracted: A 19-year-old man arrested after refusing to answer questions in court was agitated, heard voices and believed he was poisoned; in hospital he was ataxic, walked around nude and thought he was still in jail; blood pressure rose from 110/64 to 160/115 on the 16th day; on the 17th day he left, improved greatly at home without medication, could not remember what had happened, said he had taken a pill sold as methadone, and a week later showed no psychosis.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 1077, right column) and continuation (p. 1078, left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors are reasonably certain the men took phencyclidine from their history of street drugs often found to contain it and from the clinical picture; no laboratory confirmation is reported. As cited from earlier literature, PCP's analgesia usually lasts 1 to 3 hours and its psychotomimetic effects 18 to 24 hours; prolonged reactions had been reported in 1 of 65 surgical patients (10 days) and in four people with chronic schizophrenia (more than 4 weeks). The authors do not know why their patients were ill for 2 to 4 weeks and list dose, slow metabolism, toxic metabolites, idiosyncrasy or precipitation or exacerbation of a schizophrenic process.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

risk_of_bias.note: Three selected case reports with no toxicology and no psychiatric histories (editors' checklist high).

indirectness.note: Worded as a description of these cases.

publication_bias.note: Unusual cases are more likely to be published; reflected in the wording that no frequency can be given.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim resting on three case reports starts low and is downgraded two levels for risk of bias (no confirmed exposure, selected cases), giving very low. It establishes only that such courses were seen, not their frequency or cause.

statement: Whether hospital treatment shortens a long psychosis after PCP cannot be said from the three case reports of Rainey and Crowder (1975), the only report read here: antipsychotic medicines (chlorpromazine, and in one man also trifluoperazine) did not visibly change the course in two men, haloperidol was stopped in the third when seizure-like episodes of rigidity began the day after his first dose, one man became calm when placed in a dim, quiet room, and all three recovered after 2 to 4 weeks, one without medication after he left hospital. The authors cite earlier reports that haloperidol or chlorpromazine together with a quiet, isolated environment had been used, and suggest haloperidol may work better than the medicines they used, but no treatment was compared with another or with none. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In three men treated in hospital in the 1970s for a long breakdown after street drugs thought to be PCP, the medicines given for psychosis did not seem to shorten it, and one man calmed down in a dim, quiet room. All three recovered in two to four weeks. Nobody compared treatments, so it is not known what helps.
population: Three young men in one US psychiatric hospital with psychoses lasting 2 to 4 weeks attributed to PCP
exposure: Antipsychotic medicines given in hospital (chlorpromazine, trifluoperazine, haloperidol) and seclusion in a dim, quiet room; doses not given here
outcome: Course and duration of the psychosis
magnitude: No comparison. Case 2: daily chlorpromazine for a week without visible change; case 3: rising doses of chlorpromazine with trifluoperazine and injected chlorpromazine described as not effective; case 1: haloperidol stopped after one day because of seizures, not an adequate trial; all recovered within 2 to 4 weeks.

evidence.locator: Case 2, 2nd paragraph (left column); Case 3, right column, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Case 2 continued to wander, undress and be incontinent despite a week of daily oral chlorpromazine and jumped from a window the day after admission; in case 3 chlorpromazine raised over 2 weeks, trifluoperazine and chlorpromazine injections as needed were not effective, he was calm and usually slept when placed in a dim, quiet, locked room, and he improved greatly at home without medication after leaving on the 17th day.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

evidence.locator: Case 1, right column, 2nd paragraph (p. 1076); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1078, left column)
evidence.extracted: In case 1 haloperidol, given 24 hours after he was first seen, was stopped the next day when seizure-like episodes of about 5 minutes began, so he did not receive an adequate trial. The authors cite earlier use of injected haloperidol or chlorpromazine with a quiet, isolated environment and suggest haloperidol may be more effective than the chlorpromazine and trifluoperazine used in cases 2 and 3; no comparison was made.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/PCP/Rainey_1975_ProlongedPsychosisThreeCases.pdf (published version, scanned copy read on rendered page images)

risk_of_bias.note: Uncontrolled case reports; treatment was not allocated or compared, and recovery may be the natural course.

grade.reasoning: Case reports start low and are downgraded two levels for risk of bias, giving very low. Insufficient evidence: with no comparison, neither benefit nor its absence can be shown; the claim records that the treatments were not tested.
